label: Chapter 2: The House of Luxembourg, 963 to 1443

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay. Siegfried has his little castle.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Then what?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Then, for about two centuries, not much.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A rocky fortress, a handful of villages, and a dynasty that married well and waited.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The long game.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The very long game. The counts slowly gathered land, and in 1136 an inheritance gave the county to Henry the Blind, count of Namur, who joined the two territories together.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Henry the Blind. Good name.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: You'll meet another one in a minute.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But the one to remember here is Henry's daughter.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Ermesinde.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Ermesinde. I like her already.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: She inherited the county in 1196, and ruled for more than fifty years, through two marriages and a great deal of politics.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: She's remembered for granting charters of freedom to the towns of her county.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Including the capital.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1244 she gave one to the city of Luxembourg.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It freed its townspeople from many of the old obligations of serfdom, and let them organize themselves as a community, with a council of their own.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: In 1244. That's early.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In a Europe where most people lived under their lord's thumb, it was a bold step.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: To this day, Luxembourg treats Ermesinde as one of its founding figures.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Good. A woman who ruled for fifty years gets her due.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Now. The little county is about to leap onto the continental stage.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: How?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: By accident, and by tragedy. In 1288, the count of Luxembourg was killed at the Battle of Worringen, in a war over who would inherit the neighboring duchy of Limburg.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: His heir was a boy of about thirteen, also named Henry.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: We know him as Henry the Seventh.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Thirteen. Yikes.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He grew up chivalrous, pious, and quietly ambitious.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And in 1308, the German king was murdered.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The electors of the empire looked around for someone who was capable, but not too powerful.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Not too powerful. Everyone's favorite job requirement.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And they chose the count of Luxembourg.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Wait. The little county on the western edge?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Suddenly, king of the Germans.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And Henry did not waste it. He arranged for his teenage son John to marry Elisabeth, the heiress of the kingdom of Bohemia, which is roughly today's Czech Republic.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: John became King of Bohemia in 1310.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So in one marriage, a small county in the Ardennes gets one of the richest crowns in central Europe.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Exactly that.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And Henry?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He marched over the Alps into Italy, and was crowned emperor in Rome in 1312.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He dreamed of restoring imperial glory.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The poet Dante, who lived through those years and pinned his hopes on Henry, wrote that a seat was waiting for him in Paradise.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Oh. That's some endorsement.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But Henry died of a fever in 1313, near Siena, and the dream died with him.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Oh, no. And his son? The new King of Bohemia?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: John the Blind.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Henry the Blind, John the Blind.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Did they run out of nicknames?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Different men, a long time apart.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Just a coincidence of the name.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: John was one of the great adventurers of the Middle Ages.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Born in Luxembourg, raised partly at the French court.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: As King of Bohemia, he was almost never home.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Where was he?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Italy. Poland. Lithuania, fighting alongside the crusading Teutonic Knights.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He loved tournaments, and he loved France.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: His daughter Bonne married the man who became King John the Second of France, and she became the grandmother of a future French king.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Busy man. When did he go blind?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: By around 1340 he had lost his sight completely.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It didn't slow him down. In 1340 he founded a fair in Luxembourg City that still exists.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Schueberfouer. It takes place every year in late August and early September, with rides, food stalls and traditional parades, and it's the biggest funfair in the country.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Wait. A blind king founded a funfair that's still running almost seven hundred years later?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Yes.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay. That's a legacy.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Now the war that defined his end.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1346, England and France were fighting what we now call the Hundred Years' War.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: John, loyal to the French, rode to the battlefield of Crécy.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Blind.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Blind. According to the old account, he asked his knights to lead him into the fight.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They tied their horses together by the reins, so he wouldn't be separated from them, and they charged straight into the English archers.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And then?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The next morning, John and his companions were found dead on the field.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: That's a hard story.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It is. And there's a tradition that the English prince we call the Black Prince, who was just sixteen, took the three ostrich feathers from John's helmet and made them his own emblem.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Historians argue about whether that's true.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But in Luxembourg, John is remembered as the great national hero.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: His body rests in the crypt of Notre-Dame cathedral in the capital.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A symbol of bravery.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Of bravery, loyalty, and a certain doomed gallantry.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: All right. Now the greatest of the Luxembourgers.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: John's eldest son. Born in Prague, baptized Wenceslas, and he took the name Charles at the French court, in honor of his godfather and uncle.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: As Charles the Fourth, he became King of Bohemia after his father's death, and in 1355 he was crowned Holy Roman Emperor in Rome.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And what kind of emperor?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A different kind. A scholar, a builder, a patient politician.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1356 he issued a famous decree called the Golden Bull, which fixed how emperors would be elected, by seven electors.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That system more or less lasted until the empire itself ended.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Wow. Centuries of rules from one decree.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And in 1348 he founded Charles University in Prague, the first university in central Europe.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And there's a bridge, isn't there?

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Everyone has a Charles Bridge photo.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He started building the stone bridge across the Vltava that still bears his name.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He turned Prague into one of the great cities of Europe.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And he didn't forget the little county where his family began.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1354, he raised Luxembourg to the rank of duchy, and installed his half-brother Wenceslas as its first duke.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So by the late fourteenth century, this is a mighty dynasty.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Its sons ruled Bohemia, and for a time Hungary, and sat on the imperial throne.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In all, four Luxembourgers held the title of ruler of the Holy Roman Empire.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Henry the Seventh, Charles the Fourth, Charles's son Wenceslas the Fourth, and Charles's other son Sigismund.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Four.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Though only three of them were actually crowned emperor in Rome.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Henry, Charles, and Sigismund.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So Wenceslas never made it to the Rome ceremony.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Right. He was never crowned there.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Which brings us to Sigismund, the last.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A shrewd, restless man. King of Hungary from 1387, and King of the Romans from 1411.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He called the great Council of Constance, which met from 1414 to 1418 and ended a split in the Catholic Church.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: That's a big achievement.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It also burned the Czech reformer Jan Hus, which triggered the Hussite wars in Bohemia.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Right. So, mixed.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Very mixed. Sigismund was crowned emperor in 1433 and died in 1437, with no surviving son.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And with that, the male line of the House of Luxembourg came to an end.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay, so what happened to the little duchy?

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Back home, in the Ardennes?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Its glamorous rulers were scattered across central Europe.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They spent most of their time in Prague, Buda, or Rome, and they rarely visited the place that made them.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So they were absentee landlords.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: To them, Luxembourg was a source of money, and they treated it that way.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They mortgaged it. They pledged it as security for loans, and passed it around among cousins and creditors.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Does the owner count include creditors?

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Because that's a lot of paperwork.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Let's say no. We'll count real owners only.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Fair. So who ended up with it?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: One of the holders was a woman named Elisabeth of Görlitz, a niece of Sigismund.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: She was widowed, remarried, and constantly short of money.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the end, she sold her rights to the most powerful figure in the region.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Ah. And that's the first real change of owner.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1443, his forces took possession of the city, reportedly by a surprise assault with the help of local nobles who were fed up with the unstable rule of the pledge-holders.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Owner count. One.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And just like that, the old era ended.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The county that had given Europe emperors and kings was now one more piece in the growing Burgundian collection of lands.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay. Before we move on, there's something I want to ask about.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The castles.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Ah. In the countryside of Luxembourg, medieval lords built castles that still stand.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The most spectacular is Vianden, on a hill above a river in the north, one of the largest feudal residences in this part of Europe.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A castle on a hill. Obviously.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the early fifteenth century, Vianden passed by inheritance to the family of Nassau.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Nassau. Why do I know that name?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It would later become the Dutch royal house.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Keep that name in mind.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Four hundred years later, it'll be central to our story.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And next, a fortress.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Next, a very big rock.
